title: Sweep Picking
goal: Sweep clean, separated arpeggios from three-string triads to six-string shapes, and link them through minor-key progressions so they sound like a solo.
assumes: You can alternate-pick single notes evenly at sixteenths around 80 BPM (Alternate Picking through its Intermediate Level covers this) and you can hammer on and pull off cleanly. You don't need any sweeping yet, and you can start at whichever Level suits you.

skills: Even alternate picking at sixteenths, 80 BPM

orderRationale: Three Levels, each open from the start, rebuilt on 2026-11-17 after the owner played the old Step 1 (two notes, mostly rests, at 50 BPM) and called it a beginner exercise nobody should have to sit through. Beginner now starts on a real sweep: a three-string A minor triad up and down in triplets, with one beat of rest only where it teaches the muting reset. It is the standard first drill in most sweep courses (one push per click, the top note repeated where the pick turns), and it already sounds like an arpeggio. Major and minor come together in the first Step because they differ by one note and hearing that note is the point. Then the turn at the top with a hammer and a pull, which is what removes the repeated note; then the three inversions and diminished; and the Level ends with a four-bar solo over a band. Intermediate skips everything under four strings: four-string shapes, then the five-string A-shape, then the E-shape with a hammer or a tap at the top, then inversions and position shifts with those shapes, and only then linking, which the owner asked for as the backbone, on three strings first because a long shape makes a bad link worse. It ends on an eight-bar etude over a band. Advanced adds six strings, wide shifts and neoclassical sequences. The comparison was against common practice (Gambale's economy and sweep method, Becker- and Malmsteen-style arpeggio studies, Troy Grady's work on pick paths): triads before long shapes, the turnaround as its own skill, the tap as an extension of the five-string shape. Chains change chord once a bar because Jam's grid is one chord to a bar. The progressions are common vocabulary and every line is written for this Path: nothing is transcribed from a song or copied from a course.
gradingLimits: Grading stops being trustworthy at about 150 ms between notes: sixteenths at 100 BPM, eighth triplets at 133, sextuplets at 66. Rungs faster than that are self-checked, whatever they look like, and the card says where grading stops. That line is a cautious policy, not a measurement. What a sweep is graded on is timing: how even the notes are, whether each one arrived, and whether extra notes crept in. Right notes are not graded anywhere on this Path: swept notes ring into each other, and a pitch read on ringing strings can fail a take that was played right, so nothing here promises them. The tests behind these numbers used synthetic tones, and no real guitar has been through them yet. The note after a slide counts as missed if it isn't heard, so bars on sliding shapes are lower; a tap counts as a note that must be heard, and a hammer or pull that isn't heard costs nothing. In practice: Beginner is graded at every rung. In Intermediate the sixteenth-note shapes stop at 100 BPM, triplet shapes at 130, and the sextuplet pickup at 65. In Advanced most of what makes the playing hard can't be graded. Sound never tells us the two things that matter most here, muting and pick path, and the Exercises say so.

steps.title: Three-string triads, up and down
steps.goal: Sweep a minor and a major triad on the top three strings, up and back down, in even triplets, with each note separate.
steps.why: This is the sweep everyone recognises: three notes of a chord in one push, A, C, E going up and E, C, A coming back. Three strings is the size every bigger shape is made of, and it's short enough to keep clean from the first day. Triplets put one sweep on every click, so the rhythm tells you where each stroke starts. You learn major and minor together because they differ by one note, and hearing that note is what turns a shape into a chord you can use.
howTo: One push per click. Going up the strings, the pick falls through the G, B and E strings in one downward motion and comes to rest on each string before it plays it. Coming back, the same in reverse: one upward pull through E, B and G.
The top note is played twice, once at the end of the push and once at the start of the pull. That repeated note is the only place the pick changes direction.

Fretting hand: lift each finger's pressure as soon as the next note sounds, without leaving the string. Picking hand: the side of the palm rests lightly on the strings you have just left. Those two together are the mute.
The A minor shape at fret 12: little finger on the G string at 14, middle finger on the B string at 13, index on the top string at 12. For C major only the G string changes, to fret 12.
steps.payoff: A minor and C major arpeggios that sound like chords being spelled out, and a four-chord progression played as sweeps, in your first session.

exercises.title: A minor: up, back, up, and listen
exercises.purpose: The whole motion on one shape: up the strings, back down, up again, then a beat of silence. The silent beat is there for the mute: if anything is still ringing, you hear it.
howTo: Triplets, one sweep to a click: up (A, C, E), back (E, C, A), up again. On the fourth click, stop the strings and bring the pick back above the G string without touching anything.
The silence is part of the Exercise. A string still sounding in it is a mute to fix, not a reason to play faster.
exercises.coachLine: I time every note and count the ones that arrive. Whether a string rang on into the silent beat is for your ears, so listen for it.

howTo: Up, back, up, back in each bar: four sweeps, twelve notes. At the bar line only the little finger moves, from fret 14 to fret 12 on the G string.
Say the chord name on each bar line. If you can hear the change before you name it, your ears are doing their job.

exercises.title: C major becomes C minor
exercises.purpose: One fret on one string, a whole change of colour: E drops to Eb on the top string, and C major turns into C minor. It's the best ear training a sweep can give you.

Play it once slowly with no click and sing the top note of each bar. That note is the third, and it is the whole difference between major and minor.

steps.title: The turn at the top: hammer and pull-off
steps.goal: Turn the sweep round at the top with a hammer and a pull, so it loops with no repeated note and no extra pick stroke.
steps.why: In the last Step the pick turned round on a repeated note. Real sweep lines don't repeat the top note: they add one more chord tone on the top string with a hammer, pull back off it, and sweep down. The hammer and the pull give the pick a moment with nothing to do, which is exactly when it changes direction, so the turn can't be heard. This loop is the sound of a sweep in a solo, and three strings is the cheapest place to learn it.
howTo: After the top string's push, the next note is a hammer-on, so the pick has nothing to do. Use that moment to turn it round.
The pull-off back is the last note before the upward push begins. Keep the pull clean: pull slightly sideways, off the string, and do not just lift.
Start with C major: its reach on the top string is three frets. The minor shapes reach five, and they come next.
steps.payoff: A triad that loops without a seam, with the turn inaudible, at a tempo you can sing along with.

exercises.title: C major, the short reach
exercises.purpose: The whole loop with the shortest top-string reach. G, C, E, then hammer to G and back.
howTo: Triplets. The first note of the loop after the first pass is an upstroke: the sweep comes back through it and turns, so you are never starting over.
exercises.coachLine: I time each note and count the ones that arrived. A quiet hammer or pull costs nothing, so don't dig in to please me.

steps.title: Triads up the neck, then diminished
steps.goal: Play the same minor and major triad in three places up the neck, and add the diminished shape, with the shifts landing on time.
steps.why: A shape you know in one place is a shape you can only use in one place. Every triad has three shapes on the top three strings, one per inversion, and between them they cover the neck, so whatever chord comes next, one of its shapes is under your hand. Diminished comes last because it sounds tense and wants to go somewhere; it is what makes a sweep sound like the fast, dramatic thing you came to this Path for.
howTo: Name the notes out loud as you practise, at least once. The spelled notes on each Exercise are there for that.
Moving between inversions, shift during the last note of the bar, and arrive on the first finger of the new shape.
Diminished seventh shapes repeat every three frets with the same four notes. You only have to learn it once.
steps.payoff: A minor and C major in three places each, and an A minor sweep resolving from its diminished neighbour that sounds like the real thing.

exercises.coachLine: A shift is where notes go missing. If they do, look at the bar lines first.

steps.title: Your first sweep solo, with the band
steps.goal: Play looped three-string triads through two progressions over a band, and a four-bar sweep solo that ends on a held note.
steps.why: Everything so far has been against a click. A band changes how it feels: the bass plays the roots, the drums carry the beat, and your arpeggios suddenly sound like a guitar solo instead of an exercise. Three strings is enough for that, and it's short enough that you can listen to the band while you play. The four-bar solo at the end is the Beginner Level's finish line.
howTo: Use direct input or headphones for a graded take. A microphone also hears the band, and that hasn't been tested.
Lock the first note of each bar to the kick drum and let the rest of the bar fall into place.
Turn the band down until your mistakes show. A loud band covers a ringing string.
steps.payoff: You play a sweep solo over a band that follows the chords and ends on a note that sings.

steps.title: Four strings
steps.goal: Add the D string without losing the separation you built on three.
steps.why: Four strings is enough for a full-sounding chord and short enough to keep clean. A longer push means more time for an earlier note to keep ringing, so it is the first real test of your muting. It's also the first place the pick travels far enough that the arm has to carry it, not the wrist.
howTo: Let the forearm carry the pick across. The wrist stays still.
The palm mute now has to travel with the pick, and the fretting hand keeps releasing each note in turn.
The bottom note is played once: you arrive on it with the upward push and leave it with a downstroke on the next string. Keep that change small.
steps.payoff: A sweep that sounds like a real chord being spelled out, at a tempo you can sing, in four shapes.

steps.title: Five strings: the root positions
steps.goal: Own the two common five-string shapes with the root on the A string, in minor and major.
steps.why: Five strings is the big sweep, the sound people mean when they say the word. There are few shapes to learn: minor from the A string, major from the A string, and the two moved around. Everything else on the fretboard is one of those at a different fret, which is why you learn only these.
howTo: Minor: root on the A string, a hammer to the third on that same string, then one note a string up to the top. Major: a chord tone below the root, hammer to the root, then one note a string.
Mute everything. With five strings moving there is more to keep silent than there are fingers: palm on the low strings, fretting fingers across the high ones.
Keep this below your speed limit. A clean five-string sweep at a modest tempo sounds better than a fast smear.
steps.payoff: The sound you came for: a five-string arpeggio up the neck and back, with every note separate.

steps.title: Five strings: the E-shape, and a tap at the top
steps.goal: Sweep the E-shape arpeggios that start on the fifth, and add a tapped note above the top of a five-string shape.
steps.why: The A-shape puts the root on the A string. The E-shape is the barre chord you already know from the low E string, swept from the A string up, so it starts on the chord's fifth. Between the two shapes you have a minor and a major arpeggio in every part of the neck, often in the same place, which is what lets a progression stay under one hand. The tap is the other half of the classic sound: one more note above the shape, played by the picking hand, so the arpeggio reaches higher than the fretting hand can stretch.
howTo: E-shape: the first note is on the A string, then one note a string up to the top, and a hammer to the top note. There's no second note on the A string, so the bottom turn is a pick turn, and the rest after each loop gives you time for it and a moment to check the mute.
Tap with the middle finger of the picking hand, holding the pick tucked against the palm. Tap firmly on the fret, then pull off slightly downward so the fretted note under it sounds.
While you tap, the fretting hand keeps holding the note you pull off to. The tap is a loud attack and it counts as a note that must be heard.
steps.payoff: Two five-string shapes per chord, and a tapped A minor sweep that reaches up to fret 20.

steps.title: The link: two shapes
steps.goal: Get from one arpeggio into the next with no gap and no extra pick stroke, slowly enough to hear the join.
steps.why: Linked arpeggios are what make a sweep sound like a solo and not an exercise, and the link is a separate skill from either shape. Almost everyone practises the shapes and hopes the join comes along. It doesn't: the join is where the pick stops, the hand arrives late and a note gets lost. So here it gets practised alone, as slowly as you like, with nothing else to think about.
howTo: A link is one small move of the fretting hand. On the top or bottom string, step from the last note of the old shape to the nearest note of the new one with a hammer, a pull or a slide. The pick does nothing at that moment.
Choose the nearest note of the new chord, not the root. Good links barely move the hand, which is why the shapes here may look unfamiliar.
Look ahead. Know the note you are stepping to before you play the note you are stepping from.
Keep muting through the change: the last note of the old shape stops as the new one sounds.
steps.payoff: You hear one line carry on across a chord change, and a chord change that happens under your fingers instead of between two shapes.

steps.title: Chains of links
steps.goal: Link four chords in a row on three strings, without stopping, in any minor key.
steps.why: Once two shapes link, the question becomes how long you can keep it going. A four-chord chain is the unit of real playing, and the minor-key loops here are the most common things you will be asked to sweep over. The moves are small, so the hard part is keeping your place: you should know which chord is next without counting.
howTo: Learn the chords by ear first. Play the progression's roots, once through, on the low strings.
Each chord's shape starts as near as it can to the last one. Don't reach for the shape you know best: reach for the nearest one.
If a link trips you, go back to two shapes and repeat that one link. Don't push through it.
steps.payoff: A four-chord minor progression comes out of one unbroken sweep, in whichever key you land on today.

steps.title: Four and five strings, linked

steps.why: The bigger the shape, the further the hand has to come back at the end of it, so links on five strings need more planning than links on three. Mixing lengths matters too, because a line of one length sounds like a pattern, and a three-string shape in the middle of big ones gives you somewhere to breathe.
howTo: Plan the link from the bottom of each shape: the last note on the A string walks to the first note of the next shape.
With five strings there's a lot to keep silent, and the mute has to travel across every change as well.
Mixed lengths: keep the beat the same when the shape gets shorter. The short shape fills the bar with two loops.
steps.payoff: A long chain over a whole progression, big enough to sound like a solo.

steps.title: Minor keys and the V chord
steps.goal: Link through the harmonic-minor movement: the major V chord pulling back to i.
steps.why: A natural-minor loop goes round forever and never needs to resolve. The major V chord is what changes that: its G# sits a half step under A and pulls back to it, and that pull is the dark, dramatic sound of metal and neoclassical playing. These progressions are shared vocabulary, and the thing to learn is the half-step move: it is the link you will come to love.
howTo: E major in A minor contains G#, a note A minor doesn't have. Find it in the shape. It is where the sound comes from.
Aim for the G# to A step at the resolution, and hear it before you play it.
Bdim to E to Am is the minor two-five-one. It is the same pull with one more chord of warning.
steps.payoff: You hear a chord pull back to the minor at the end of a sweep, and a progression sounds like it's going somewhere.

steps.goal: Use a sweep as part of a line that goes somewhere, starting and ending in a scale or on a held note.

steps.title: Six strings
steps.goal: Own a clean six-string sweep from the low E, minor and major, and link passes across all six.
steps.why: Six strings is the longest push you can make, and it is a real physical challenge, since the arm travels the whole width of the neck and every string behind the pick has to stay quiet. It adds less new music than the step from three to five did. Come to it for the sound and for the discipline: a clean six-string sweep shows up any weakness in your muting at once.
howTo: The arm does this. The wrist stays quiet, and the forearm carries the pick from the low E to the high E in one long push.
Muting is the whole game: palm on what's behind the pick, the fretting fingers rolling off what's in front of it. Low strings ring loudest, so check them first.
Grading on these is limited: only the slowest rungs are graded, and even those have never been tried on a real guitar.
steps.payoff: A sweep from the lowest note on the guitar to near the highest, with every note separate.

steps.goal: Jump between shapes far apart on the neck, and play sweeps fast enough that grading no longer applies.
steps.why: Everything until now has moved a fret or two. Sometimes a line needs an octave jump, and that's a throw of the whole arm that has to land exactly. This is also where speed comes in, so it's where the app can't help much: you'll be working by recording and by ear, as players always have.
howTo: Look at the landing spot before you leave. The hand follows the eye.
A shift is one fast movement and then stillness. Land early and let the note come to you.
Fast rungs are self-checked. Record yourself and slow the recording down: nothing is more honest than that.
steps.payoff: A line that jumps the neck, and a burst of sweep at a speed you couldn't have played a month ago.

steps.title: Neoclassical sequences
steps.goal: Play the moves that give this style its sound: diminished shapes climbing in minor thirds, and triads walking up the harmonic minor scale.
steps.why: Baroque-flavoured metal comes from a few harmonic ideas played very fast: the major V, the diminished seventh on its leading tone, and triads walked in sequence. You've met the first two. A sequence adds the sense of a long line unfolding, and a diminished chord that moves three frets at a time is the most fun you can have with one shape.
howTo: A diminished seventh is the same four notes every three frets. So G#dim7, Bdim7, Ddim7 and Fdim7 are one sound in four places.
In a sequence, hear each bar as the next step of one melody. The top notes usually tell the tale.
These are original lines in a shared style, and meant as starting points: write your own as soon as you can.
steps.payoff: The unmistakable sound of a neoclassical run, in lines you can change and call your own.

levels.title: Intermediate: four and five strings, then linking
levels.summary: No two-string basics: start on four- and five-string arpeggios, the A-shape and the E-shape with a hammer or a tap at the top, then move them around the neck, link them through minor-key progressions, and finish with an eight-bar etude over a band.

startHereIf: You can loop a three-string minor triad with a hammer and a pull, cleanly, at 100 BPM triplets.
On a recording of that loop, each note stops as the next one starts.

Three strings feel easy, and four or five strings come out as a smear.

warmups.title: A progression of the day
warmups.purpose: A four-chord chain through a different minor progression and key each time. It's linked sweeps, gently, and it never repeats tomorrow what it did today.
howTo: Start well under your clean tempo. Nothing here should feel hard, and it plays different notes each day.

levels.title: Advanced: the whole neck, at speed
levels.summary: Six strings, wide shifts and neoclassical sequences. Grading runs out early here: most of what makes this hard can only be judged by ear and on a recording.

startHereIf: You can chain four five-string shapes through a minor progression without stopping, at 90 BPM triplets.
A recording of that take is free of ringing strings.
